content: Technological inputs play a critical role in shaping the performance of digital health systems. The iterative nature of technology development, often referred to in engineering as the spiral model of software development and enhancement, involves repeated cycles of prototyping, testing, and refinement. This process is informed by feedback from end-users, ensuring that the technology evolves to meet their needs effectively. In the context of digital health interventions, these systems offer significant potential benefits, including improved efficiency in health service delivery, enhanced data collection, and the ability to provide and exchange information on demand. This facilitates communication across various levels of the health system and among providers, ultimately improving the coordination and quality of care. Indicators used to evaluate digital health interventions extend beyond simple coverage rates. They measure service utilization outputs and health outcomes at different stages—early, intermediate, and advanced—across three levels of health service delivery: the client, the provider, and the health system. These indicators are designed to address specific constraints at each level, such as availability, cost, technical efficiency, quality, and utilization of health services. At the client level, indicators assess the direct impact of digital health interventions on individuals who benefit from the services. This includes outcomes such as improved health knowledge, timely care-seeking behavior, and reduced illness duration. For example, programs like the Mobile Alliance for Maternal Action (MAMA) or m4RH focus on behavior change communication at the client level, requiring targeted indicators to measure their effectiveness. At the provider level, indicators evaluate the impact of digital health systems on healthcare workers, including their knowledge, efficiency, and adherence to care standards. For instance, programs like cStock, which aim to reduce drug stock-outs, require indicators that measure performance across clients, providers, and the health system as a whole. At the health system level, indicators assess the broader impact of digital health interventions on system-wide efficiency, cost savings, and quality of care. These include measures of cumulative time savings for healthcare providers, reductions in data entry errors, and improvements in resource allocation. Cost-related indicators are essential for understanding the financial implications of digital health interventions. These include both the direct costs of implementation and the costs averted due to timely and appropriate care. For example, timely identification of illnesses can prevent disease progression, reducing the financial burden on both clients and the health system. Cost savings can also result from reduced transportation costs, fewer manual data entry requirements, and more efficient use of human resources. Technical efficiency is another critical dimension, focusing on achieving desired outputs with minimal inputs. At the client level, this includes reduced time to receive care and shorter illness durations. At the provider level, it involves optimizing the allocation of time between clinical and administrative tasks. At the health system level, technical efficiency is measured by cumulative time savings across all providers. Data collection for these indicators often requires additional surveys or the use of back-end timestamps in digital health systems. Quality of care is assessed through three dimensions: structure, process, and outcome. Structure refers to the resources and organizational framework supporting care delivery. Process involves the activities carried out during care provision, while outcome measures the impact of services on health. Quality indicators may also encompass dimensions such as effectiveness, efficiency, acceptability, and equity. Improvements in service quality at the client level often result from enhanced efficiency and knowledge at the provider level, as well as client-reported responses to health reminders. In summary, digital health interventions have the potential to transform healthcare delivery by improving efficiency, quality, and accessibility. However, their success depends on rigorous monitoring and evaluation using well-defined indicators that address constraints across all levels of the health system.
